utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Before you bring in the witness, we thought that we would talk with counsel about final submissions. We are getting close to the end of the trial. Hopefully, the Defence will be finished this week, if not next week; probably it will carry over to next week. Then we will recess for a week and then the Prosecution will present its rebuttal. What the Judges wanted were written submissions, if you can submit them, but certainly oral closing arguments. We were trying to come up with possible dates. I would like you to just think about what we are thinking about, and then discuss it with each other and tell us either at the end of today or tomorrow. The courtroom will be in use by the other Trial Chamber on 19th and 20th November. So there is a possibility for us to begin closing arguments on Thursday, November 21st, or if counsel would not be ready by that date, we could begin the following week, either on Monday, 25th or Tuesday, 26th. I do not know how much time you think that you would need for your closing arguments. We want to encourage you to make them as full as possible, that is for sure, but that is just what we were thinking. The Prosecution had said you thought you would need a week for your rebuttal. So if we finish up with the Defence case by 30th of this month, that would be two days next week, then we would be in recess until 6th or so November, is that right? Then if the Prosecution was to begin that week, on Thursday, it may be a little difficult, only because it is towards the end of the week, but if you began that Thursday and finished up by 15th -- I have a calendar before me, so if you do not have a calendar, just kind of think about it -- if you could give your submissions beginning November 21st, that would be good. If not, it would be the following week, but we certainly need to finish submissions -- the absolute latest -- would be November 29th, but it would be our desire to finish up on 28th November. So think about how you think you could proceed, and let us know this evening or tomorrow. It depends upon how much time the Prosecution needs but, as I say, if we spent two days of next week on the Defence case and finish on 30th, then we could begin with the Prosecution's case either on November 7th or the following week, but the only problem with beginning the following week is -- that is the week of 11th -- that the Trial Chamber 1 needs the courtroom on 19th and 20th. So, let us know and we will see if we can schedule something. OK. Miss Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. One other issue about closing argument: will the Judges allow the Prosecution and the Defence to have the option of having more than one person argue for closing argument?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I do not have a problem. No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So that would be an option we would have?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes. We want the fullest closing arguments as possible. However it is done is up to you, but it has been a long trial and there is a lot of evidence that we have received but, yes, you may do. So more than one counsel for each side may give closing arguments. Would you bring in the witness, please? LJUBOMIR TADIC, recalled

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Judge Stephen is reminding me to encourage you to give us as much analysis or schedules or outlines that you wish. Make it easy! Mr. Tadic, you understand that you are still under the oath that you took yesterday to tell the truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Thank you. Mr. Kay, you may begin. Examined by MR. KAY, continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, yesterday at the end of the day you told us about opening your business in part of the family home in Kozarac. What exactly was your business?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the sale of alcoholic and non-alcoholic beverages on a wholesale basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When did you open that business?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I opened it -- I remember very well -- 15 days, roughly, ahead of the outbreak of the conflict in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you opened your business had you stocked it with beverages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In those 15 days that it was open, was it trading every day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Almost every day. I sold very quickly my stocks that I had brought in by truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Who was working in the shop doing the selling to customers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would come, and the goods were brought in by truck from the brewery because I had a contract with the Banja Luka brewery and it was their duty to supply me with beer, and the other beverages I purchased myself in Banja Luka, and I transported them by van.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When was the last day that that business traded in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The last day I was on Wednesday 20th in Banja Luka, and my wife called the brewery up and they told me that beer would be delivered the next day on 21st May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you go to the shop on 21st May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you receive a delivery on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I came roughly an hour and a half ahead of the arrival of the truck. I came by bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: On that day how much was delivered by the brewery to the shop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 300 crates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was that of beer or beer and soft drinks or just soft drinks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only beer, 300 crates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you trade after 21st May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before that I had received three truck loads of beer from the Banja Luka brewery and, for instance, I would get one or two truck loads in a week and it would sell in two or three days, because the local people, there were many cafes in Kozarac, and it suited their interests to buy from me, simply because the price of the beer was far lower than if they went to Banja Luka or Prijedor. Then they would have additional transportation costs, and they were able to purchase from me at a slightly higher price than the factory price in the brewery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you go into the shop on 22nd May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 21st May with the truck of the Banja Luka brewery I went to Banja Luka about 3.00, 3.30, and I carried with me my TV, a colour TV, belonging to Dusko Tadic and a small, dark terrier -- he was in a box -- and I put all that on the truck and with the driver I went to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Why were you taking the television and the small terrier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was Dusko's, both the terrier and the TV set, and the family was in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So it was for the family in Banja Luka that you were taking the terrier and the ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, for Dusko's wife and mother and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Why could you not return to the shop on 22nd May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 21st, when I left for Banja Luka, I gave Dusko the key of my business premises, and I told him if he needed anything, some beer for his cafe, be free to take it and if somebody would come -- I did not have people to work there on a regular basis; I had a boy to help me unload -- but I said if anyone comes to buy some drinks, sell it to them. He knew the price and so on. On 22nd, and I told him I would come on the 22nd, for us to sell all that over the weekend. However, the next day when I got up I heard that everything was blocked, that it was not possible to head in the direction of Kozarac or Prijedor, nor was it possible to go from Prijedor to Banja Luka, that Kozarac was under blockade, a conflict had still not broken out, but that there was a possibility of a conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The premises next door to you were Dusko Tadic's cafe, when did that start trading as a cafe, can you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It started trading, I think, at the end of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In that period from 1990 to ----

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In that period until 1992, were all ethnic groups in Kozarac welcome to go into that cafe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they would come to the cafe. I would come often because before I opened my shop I had to transfer the living space into business premises, so I had to have the plans, I had to get authorisation, so that I would come often. I had to go to the Prijedor municipality, to the authorities, to get permission for this. When the cafe started working many people would come, local people, people of Kozarac, many whom I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was it a cafe where only Serbs were welcome?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there were very few Serbs in Kozarac, maybe 10 families in the centre of Kozarac. So that 95 per cent of the population of Kozarac were Muslims. There were a few Croats also.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were there any Muslim employees who worked at your brother's cafe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were several waiters. I think the son of Adil Jakupovic was working there, the son of Kahrimanovic, the former director of the elementary school in Kozarac and the last waiter working there was a fair boy. He was a Muslim too. Also in the meantime there was a Serb working too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What was Dusko Tadic's relationship like with the other people in Kozarac in this period from 1991/92?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusko had continued to have good relations with a large number of local people, and especially with the younger people who would come to his cafe. The older people were not such frequent visitors. It was not a restaurant. It was a nice, modern cafe that young people came to, and with most people he had very good relations, with the older ones too because he had a coffee making machine for espresso coffee so that older people would like to have a cup of coffee outside or inside in the morning -- a machine that others did not have at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: During this same period, were you regularly visiting Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I said that I went to Kozarac in the period 1991 and '92. I went in '89 and before as well, but because of this business I had, I had to go frequently. I would take Friday off, Saturday, Sunday, when I was working on my business premises. When I completed building works, then I would come on Thursday, Friday, or on some other days, depending on when deliveries were due.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In the period of '91 to '92 was Kozarac the same in its atmosphere as it had been in former years that we have heard about in Court as being a happy place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well you see, Kozarac is a nice place. I love it. I grew up there. I live there. I spent my childhood there. I like to go there now. My children like to go there. Something draws us to go there and I will always be going there, regardless who will be living there. My mother is still alive and my brother comes, and even when they are gone I will go on going there because it was really a nice place to live in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But did that atmosphere change in 1991/1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, after the death of our father in '89, soon after that, one could feel certain changes, especially in 1991 it was quite pronounced. Simply some of those people -- I personally was not insulted by anyone, but one could feel a distance. Some of them would not answer when we bid them "good day". I was surprised. How come? We had never had any disputes or quarrels. But one could live there still in that period, but Dusko -- I was not familiarised with that immediately, Dusko did not tell me straightaway, but he told me later, two months later after this letter, he got a threatening letter. He did not tell anyone straightaway. Afterwards he said he did not know what to do, whether he should tell someone or not. He did not know what to do, but he told me about this letter which he had received. I may be wrong in the exact date. I think it was on 5th September 1990. I remember the text of the letter. I saw the letter. It was on an ordinary piece of paper, and it said: "The holy war, a brother for the jihad, the holy war", and underneath: "We cannot wait any longer, you must move out within three months otherwise we will kill your family, your children, both children and you. There is not a chance for you to survive", something to that effect. It said: "Your wife has proven to be one of us", something to that effect and signed, "Young Muslims, SDA, Kozarac", and there was something in Arabic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Had you ever had any experience of anything like this before, any previous threats in such a way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What effect did this have on your brother, this letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably he was afraid. He was wondering what to do. You know how it is, the Serbs were a minority in Kozarac. I think the ratio was 95 per cent Muslims and five per cent Serbs and others -- of course there was fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Have you been a member of any political parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a member of the Communist Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But were many people members of the Communist Party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a member of the Communist Party from 1978 and this was a mass movement because there was no other party. More or less in all work organisations it was required that we join and those who did not, they were looked upon as being ethnically coloured.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to other political parties, have you ever been a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the Communist Party collapsed or, rather, when Yugoslavia fell apart, I cannot remember exactly but I think at the end of 1991 I joined the SDS in Banja Luka. I do not just know the date exactly. I think it was 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: To join the SDS in Banja Luka did you have to pay a membership fee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You would have to fill in a form with your data and a very insignificant amount as a fee, but, yes, you did have to pay a membership fee.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was that an annual fee that had to be paid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, an annual fee.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you ever repay your fee after the first time of joining?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I joined the SDS simply because the former party had been disbanded. The first to be formed was SDA, then HDZ and then when the Serbian Democratic Party was formed Serbs normally joined en masse, but afterwards I was never politically committed. I truly was not interested in politics because I thought politics was dangerous, and one can suffer through politics. So I was not one that was engaged in politics at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you ever go to any meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Or read any literature about the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you ever have political discussions with your brother Dusko about the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but I told him once on one occasion: "Dusko, take care, think how our father fared even though he was a member of the Communist Party".

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I meant was the following: our father was a combatant from 1941. He was an officer. He was wounded several times. He was a partisan, of course, and in the former Yugoslavia during the time of the war, as you probably know, there were Ustashas, there were Chetniks, there were partisans. Our father was arrested twice in 1941 in Kozarac as a communist, as a partisan. In '92, upon the formation of the first proletarian battalion. They were meant to go to Eastern Bosnia, a selected group of them, some 10 or so of them, and when they were to join this Unit they were first near Kotor Varos and he was heavily wounded by a grenade. He was transferred to a hospital in Josani near Celinac. He was lying in hospital. There were 70 or so wounded partisans. They were guarded by a unit from Celinac. In the night, I do not know the date, anyway around midnight -- my father told me this -- a group of Chetniks broke in and slaughtered these wounded men. My father survived by chance because he was lying behind the door which was -- when they opened that door they fired machine gunfire. Some were killed, others jumped out of the window, and he crept under the bed and he dragged the body of one of the killed patients on top of him. Then he took out their bayonets and they went from one to another piercing them and, having pierced this dead man, they also injured our father under the chin and here at the waist. He pretended to be dead. Some had jumped out of the window but they were caught, and in the morning when it dawned, the survivors were lined up in front of the hospital. There was some exchange of fire, then other partisans who had not been wounded carried out an attack. The Chetniks fled, and our father managed to save his life. As for the counsel I gave him, these were the reasons. Because after the war our father who had these great merits, he was wounded five or six times in the war, he did not have much in the sense of rewards. There were medals awarded. There were many that he did not get. Among the privileges he had were simply that nobody interfered with him, but he would not go into politics, whereas many others would appropriate other people's merits. So he paid dearly for his political commitment because, though he was an officer in the war, he ended up as a watchman at the factory in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The translation we had on the transcript said '92, do you mean 1942?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Of course. All this was happening in 1942 when our father had these problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In November of 1991 there was a plebiscite in Kozarac organised by the SDS for the Serbian people, and your brother Dusko was the organiser of it within Kozarac. Were you involved in that in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know if in 1991 the SDS had any sizeable body of people in support of it in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was it visible as a political party? Was it a party within that town that had a great voice, that promoted its views amongst people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It played no role in Kozarac because Kozarac, as far as I know, it was -- it had about 25, 26,000 inhabitants and it was predominantly Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What about the SDA, the other political party that was a dominant force in the region, can you tell us about what sort of voice and presence that had in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, all functions in the Local Commune, in the local government, had SDA. It was a strong party with a large number of members. There were a lot of members. Not everybody, but a lot of them were members of SDA, and they were putting out large placards at the entrance of Kozarac with pictures of Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did this have any effect upon the minority Serb population within that town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably it caused some fear in 1991. One could sense that everybody is closing in to be with their own, but let me make it clear. In Kozarac, the Muslims, even though the Muslims were members of SDA, they were not all extreme in their views. They were nice people, honest people, but they just joined their own people and their party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did there come a stage in 1992 before the conflict in Kozarac that certain families started leaving the town to move elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was a period, the period in 1992 and late 1991 less, but it was more in 1992. There were moving families, those who had somebody elsewhere, somebody abroad, and many were abroad. Almost every household had a member abroad and, more or less, they all were well to do. So, one could notice, and our house was in the centre, on the main street, so you could notice these departures; mostly it was women and children and some of the elderly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were these Serb families as well as Muslim families who were leaving the region in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, seeing that Muslims were leaving, probably fearing the war, also the Serb families took their children away from Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At this time there was a war going on in Croatia and the forces of the former Yugoslavia were involved in fighting troops in Croatia. Was this a matter that was in the minds of the people in Kozarac during this period of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did there come a time when Dusko Tadic's family also left Kozarac for a period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you tell us when that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was at the beginning of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Which members of the family left Kozarac at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All members left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did that include Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but together with Dusko there was an Orthodox priest with his family who left in the same car.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know where they went, the Tadic family, when they left Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Where did they go to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They came to me in Banja Luka, both the priest with his family and Dusko with his own.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Dusko's family, did that include his wife Mira, the two children and your mother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did Dusko Tadic stay in Banja Luka or did he return to Kozarac, having left with his family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusko returned the next day, back to Kozarac, and the priest, Mladen Majkic, in his car went to Sanski Most in the -- to Kozice is the name of the settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Dusko Tadic's wife, Mira, the children and your mother, did they remain in Banja Luka or go elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they arrived they stayed the night with me, all of them, the priest and his family and Dusko and the mother and children. The apartment was very small, only 34 square metres, so that we did not have much room, but we sort of laid down mattresses and so they somehow spent the night. The priest left in his own car and Dusko left not that very moment but later to Kozarac, and I, I cannot say exactly whether it was that day or the next day, in my white van, it was a Volkswagen, a bit older, because the Orthodox priest told them, "Come to me, there is a house there so you can be there, to that place Kozice", so I took them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is that Mira, the children and your mother that you took to Kozice in the combi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What vehicles did you own at this time, Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had a van, a Volkswagen, an older type, I think it was May -- the make was 79 or '80. I had a motorcycle -- Ford Escort, sorry, that I bought in Germany and I brought it to Banja Luka with me, but there was something wrong with the carburettor and I could not find a part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have on the transcript here: "I had a motorcycle, Ford Escort, sorry", did you have a motorcycle, a motor bike?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no. It was a Ford Escort 1300 cubic, and red in colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I think there may have been a translation problem there. Having taken the family of Dusko to Kozice, did they return to Kozarac at any stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They returned somewhere. They were there for quite a while, I think about on 29th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How long did they stay in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I came to Kozarac, I think, on the 1st. I know that Dusko told me, "Here, we got here, and here we go again, there is a problem", because I think at that time I heard that at that time the power was taken over by the Serb police in Prijedor, and there was a panic in Kozarac because Kozarac was part of the Prijedor municipality, and in the past it used to be its own municipality and then later it was joined.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Having said to you about the trouble that had occurred by the takeover, did the family of Dusko Tadic remain in Kozarac long or did they move?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, in the meantime Dusko and I, since he was coming on several occasions still, he told me -- in fact, I told him that there was a possibility that I find temporary lodging for him, that a friend of mine who worked with me at one time in Cajavec -- his name was Nihad Alic -- that his brother has the keys to a house near his own house, and he was watching the house because I think the woman who was an Ukrainian went to Germany and was not planning on coming back any time soon, and that house had been robbed several times, he said. So, he would like -- he asked, called the woman on the phone and he said that he had a friend who, that he would bring him there temporarily, that there is nothing to worry, that everything would be all right, that he was honest, that nothing would be missing; and she agreed that he give him the key -- that he gives the key to Dusko Tadic. When I told him that, he said: "Well, let's then do that, see what the situation is like. They are leaving, so who knows what can happen?" So then from the moment of arrival in Kozarac they were there for three days and then they came.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So the house you are talking about that your friend Alic was aware of, was that in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So what happened then? Did the Tadic family after a few days in Kozarac leave Kozarac and go to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you tell us whenabouts this was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three days, somewhere between 1st -- no, it was not the 1st. They came on 29th April. I think around 3rd May or 4th May. I do not know exactly, but in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The family that left Kozarac at that time, was that the wife Mira, the children and your mother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did Dusko Tadic go with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that he brought them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you see them when they arrived in Banja Luka having left Kozarac then in early May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They came to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So did they go to your house first before going to the house elsewhere in Banja Luka that the man Alic had made available?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They came to my house and then immediately we went to see that house, and that house was not finished. It was a huge house, had a top floor, but nothing was finished on the top floor. There was only raw space. It was not ready to be inhabited, but the bottom of the house, like the basement, there was -- it was furnished, there was one large room and there was a kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: To get to the part of the house then, the basement, how would you get to that part of the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was the Koste Jarica Street where that house was. You could get there by car all the way up to the entrance. There was a fence and when you walk in from the facade it was -- it was blocked and so you had to go around, so you had to go all the way around, and then come from the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is that at the back of the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I would like you now to look at some photographs, D62A, please, and D62B. If they could be put on the monitor straightaway beside the witness? Thank you very much. Do you recognise the photograph on the left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is that the house you have been telling us about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you could park the car and that was the entrance and this is the front of the house. There was nothing finished. None of this was finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The photograph on the right, what does that show?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It shows the back of the house. You had to go around this way and down and then you go around and come -- there were some vines there and I think there was some water there, maybe it was a pipe, and then there was the entrance to the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How close to where you lived was this house in Koste Jarica Street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One could say maybe a kilometre, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The man Alic who told you of this house and made it available, where did he live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He lived, you see from here, this house, you continue on this side there is another one and then across from that house to the left was Alic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know a man called Dragoje Balte?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dragoje Balte.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am sorry. But do you know who I am speaking of when I mention that name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, and where does he live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He lived -- it is like this, the next house over was a smaller house and it was a back house, and next one over was Dragoje Balte's house, but both those were the property of Dragoje Balte.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps if you could look at photograph 62C and if that could be put on the monitor straightaway? That third photograph, do you recognise where that photograph has been taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the house of Dragoje Balte, but from the other side, this is the balcony, the one on the back of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we see there the house that Dusko Tadic and his family moved into in Banja Luka? If so, can you put the pointer on the spot and hold it there for about five seconds?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the house and you can only see the roof.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know Dragoje Balte before they moved into that house in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How long did the family stay in that house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the date of their move in they stayed maybe a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did Dusko Tadic remain at the house living with the family there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What happened to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We spent a lot of time together at that time -- that was the period between 3rd May and May 16th -- and we saw each other a lot. We would sit together, have a drink. He would bring the mother and the children to my place and to my wife's mother. One was in the street of Koste Jarica and behind it was the street of Milosa Duica, and then he was bringing the mother, especially the mother, to Jovo Samardzija. That is an elderly man, a veteran, and his wife is related to our mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You said in answer to the question, did Dusko Tadic remain at the house living with the family there, no; so where was he after the family moved in on 3rd May? You have told us how he spent his time, but did he return to Kozarac to continue with the cafe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We are talking now about 3rd May. You told us that you had opened your cafe at the beginning of May and that you were trading ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: --- from your cafe until 21st May. In that period that you were trading at your cafe, was Dusko Tadic still working at his cafe in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I made a mistake. Dusko Tadic, when he brought the family, he went back to Kozarac, and his cafe work was open all the way up until May 22nd, 23rd, up until the eve of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So in that period from 3rd May until 23rd May, did he also return to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did he visit his family that remained in that house that you have shown us in Koste Jarica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The conflict in Kozarac started on 24th May. Do you know where Dusko Tadic was on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 24th May Dusko was in Banja Luka and on 23rd May he was in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How do you know he was in Banja Luka on 23rd May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I already said that from May 22nd, a Friday, I remember that because I remember it, but I also have a document saying when a delivery arrived from the Banja Luka brewery, that was the 21st, and I went to Banja Luka. I was to go back the next day. Everything was blocked and it was not possible to go in or out of Kozarac. I was worried. I wanted to go but I did not know how to get there. I knew he had -- he was there alone and I was afraid for him, but there was no way for me to go there. However, he appeared on 23rd of May in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Where did you see him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He came to my place briefly, and he told me: "I only just managed to escape alive. Here I am. I came by train". He said he came by train from Prijedor in the afternoon, this was, and he even said that some Muslims living in Prijedor had come to Banja Luka, among others, my school friend and a childhood friend, Tadic Esad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So having left Kozarac, as you say, on 23rd May, were you aware in Banja Luka of the conflict that started in Kozarac on the afternoon of 24th May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So, having left Kozarac on 23rd May, as you have told us your brother did, were you aware of the conflict that broke out in that town of Kozarac in the afternoon of 24th May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kozarac is 45 kilometres from Banja Luka and news would spread quickly, and there were reports on the media, on the radio. What was said was that Kozarac was under blockade, that Muslim authorities or, rather, units would not surrender their weapons and a conflict had broken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you take part in any of the fighting or attack on Kozarac in that period from 24th May onwards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. If I wanted to, I could have joined in a unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: On 24th May onwards, during the period of the conflict of about five days, something like that, do you know where your brother Dusko Tadic was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From 23rd May Dusko was all the time in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My flat and the house in which Dusko was staying is removed one kilometre away on the outside. In between is the family home of my wife. There were several cafes in between, and who was closer to him than me, he would come often. I would pass by too. We would sit down in one of those cafes or a pizzeria. For instance, there was a pizzeria, another one called "Bel Ami" and several such places and particularly in the evenings we would go out to have a drink.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Having arrived in Banja Luka for this period then, from 23rd May, how long did Dusko Tadic remain living in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, I did not understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Having arrived in Banja Luka on 23rd May, for how long did Dusko Tadic remain living in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until June 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Why do you say until June 16th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the area of Prijedor there were the war operations, and if he were to go there he would be snatched up by our military police and taken to one of the units. In Banja Luka he was safe and he could stay there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you mobilized on any particular date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in the reserves of -- that was the Territorial Defence, like the Muslims in Kozarac, they had Territorial Defence units, and so there was a Serbian Territorial Defence too. I was a reserve from April 5th until June 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you say that you were a reserve, was that within Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What were your duties then from April until June 16th as a reserve in Banja Luka, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing really, because it is a Territorial Defence unit, not a war unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is all right. I am just asking -- you are facing to me -- that the microphone that is closest to me is switched on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing in particular. I did not have any special duties. It is a Territorial Defence unit that I was in. Our duty, because we were on the territory of the Local Commune of Starcevici, we had to provide security for the most important edifices in that part of Banja Luka. Such units existed in the part of Banja Luka called Mejdan, another district called Laus, another one called Centar and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So what did you do in relation to these edifices?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were quite a number of us mobilized, so that I had to protect, watch over, the elementary school, to be on guard in front of the school. Then there was a bridge at Rebrovci, then there was the Orthodox church, buildings like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How often would you report for these duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One day I would perhaps have four hours on duty. Then I would be free for 24 hours or 48 hours. It depended really, because there was no war. The situation was not a dangerous one at the time that you would have to be present all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Doing these duties were they voluntary work by you or were you required to join the reserve at this time with other people and guard these edifices?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I was working in Cajavec I was a member of the civil defence. That existed at the level of work organisations. When I left Cajavec, I had to belong somewhere, so that I had to report to the Local Commune, and then they assigned us to Territorial Defence units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 16th June was a date that you said you were mobilized. Was that a general mobilization for everyone or a particular date upon which you were mobilized?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: June 16th was the date of a general mobilization called in the territory of what was then the Autonomous Region of Krajina or, in fact, Banja Luka, the whole region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So was that a general mobilization that applied to most people or only some people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most people, almost all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your mobilization took what form? Did you join the military or the police or any other organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence Unit existed in the territory of Starcevici, the Local Commune of Starcevici, was automatically transferred to a wartime unit. Territorial Defence units were abolished and a 2nd Light Infantry Brigade was formed which included those territorial units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your brother Dusko, do you know where he was mobilized to, what duties he had to do? Where did he go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We knew about 10 days in advance that there would be a general mobilization. In view of the fact that he was in the Prijedor records, his place of mobilization was Prijedor. So he had to report in Prijedor. There already existed war units that had waged war in Slavonia, the 5th Kozara, the 43rd Kozara brigades, and he had to report to the military staff and then he got a wartime assignment. He told me that he did not want to join a military unit. He had no experience. He had no will and I think he was afraid to go to the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So do you know how he was mobilized?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What did he join?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He came to my apartment and he said he would like best to join the traffic police, if possible. Then we called up Radovan Vokic, our uncle's son, who was an active duty policeman, I called him up and then he spoke to him. He said, he asked him whether he could fix it through our godfather, Jankovic Dusan, so that he would be positioned in the traffic police. Then I took the earphone and I said: "Please help, help us, if not he will have to go to a combat unit. He would go to Slavonia. Who knows what would happen?". Then he promised to do what he could. After that, we called several more times and he said he had spoken to Jankovic and this was by then the day before the official mobilization. He told him: "Come immediately and you will get a position in the traffic police".

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So that would have been 15th June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: During this period then from 23rd May until the mobilization on 16th June, did you visit Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: On how many occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you visit Kozarac with your brother Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was it on those two occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: First of all, can you tell us about the first time of a visit to Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would first like to say that I had heard that Kozarac had been destroyed and I wanted to see what had happened to our family home. Of course, a truck load of goods was there. There was Dusko's cafe and all the facilities inside. So we talked about it and said: "Shall we go?" and we decided to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you tell me when you first visited Kozarac after the conflict had happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went, it was 1st or 2nd May -- no, sorry, 1st or 2nd June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How long did you leave Banja Luka for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went that day to Omarska, the railway station. We went by train and from there we walked to Lamovita. It is a village on the road, on the highway, Prijedor to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What time did you leave Banja Luka on the train?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you tell me the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not know. It was early, 9.00, 10.00, 8.00 maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You mentioned Omarska railway station. How close to the camp that was sited at Omarska is that railway station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know at the time, because I had never been there. But afterwards, after the conflict, after all this, after Dusko's arrest, I went there, but then there was no camp. I had no idea what it was like and that was the first time I saw it. But I think the distance is up to three kilometres, the last building, the restaurant, the big hall, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is that on the Kozarac side of the railway line or the other side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The other side, and from the train you could see some of the buildings that also belonged to the mine, and you could read "Iron ore mine Ljubija". It was on the left-hand side moving from Banja Luka to Prijedor, on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was there any indication to you at Omarska railway station that there was this camp in the former Ljubija mine site?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the station, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You told us that you walked to Lamovita. What happened at Lamovita?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We reached the crossroads. Then we went on. This is the crossroads of the Prijedor to Banja Luka and Lamovita/Omarska roads. Then we went to one of Dusko's former waiters. His name was Timarac. They called him "Pile". His nickname was "Pile".

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How good are you with maps, Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Answer not translated].

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let us try then. Prosecution Exhibit 280, please. If this could be placed in front of you so that you can familiarise yourself with it? Can you see in the middle of this map we have the big lake called Sanicani?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you see on the right-hand side of the map we have the village of Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you see further up the map where Kozarac is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are you able to indicate to us where on this map Lamovita is that you spoke of? See if you can, and if you cannot then we will not show it on the screen, but if you can, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is not written on this map as a village or place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not written, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, it is not written, but would you be able to point where it would be found?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can. I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If that could be put on the screen to your right? With that steel indicator, can you point to us where Lamovita would be found? Can the map be put so that it is right over? Yes. Move it more to your right, my left. I wish I could control this myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: I think the map D79 will help a great deal. It is marked there, Lamovita.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am grateful to your Honour. If we can see if the witness can point out? Can you move the map further across, please? Can you point to where Lamovita would be found? There.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [The witness indicated] This is the junction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That is the crossroads there. Is that road that comes from Omarska ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: --- meeting there what is known as the new Banja Luka/Prijedor highway?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Left is to Prijedor, right to Banja Luka, up there is Lamovita. There is a little bit more road and then there is a small petrol pump there. Here, Lamovita is here somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Is there a district known as Lamovita in addition to the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I do not know if we have ever actually had the camp site of Omarska pointed out to us. We have heard that it is some, perhaps, three kilometres from the village. If the witness still has 280 in front of him?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, I think we did many, many weeks ago, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps it is good to have our memories refreshed. If 280 could be put back in front of the witness? Mr. Tadic, it would be right to say that since all these matters you visited the site of where the camp was at Omarska on several occasions, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, and after 1994, I suspect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, after.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are you able to point out to us where that site is on this map in front of you? Omarska is on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let us see. You see, there was an overhead, then you go to the left and there was a big red building with the words inscribed on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I stop you there? Can you point to it on the map for us? That is what we want. We know where it is and what it looks like, but we want to identify it on the map if you can do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somewhere here, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we can just try that and see where it is. Perhaps, usher, if you can put it back on the monitor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here it is. Here, somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Keep your eye on that and if you could put the steel pointer on the place, and if you could have the bottom half of the map right up on the monitor and if you could put Omarska in the middle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is somewhere here, the first part. Then it goes on here. [The witness indicated] There is this large complex. I do not know exactly, but from the railroad in this direction three kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You see the yellow road that runs south of Omarska through Reljici, yes? If you went down that road, where would you find the camp of Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you just keep the pointer on for five seconds?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somewhere there. [The witness indicated]. I am simply not very good with maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You have answered one question anyway. Your Honour, I think that is an appropriate moment looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You have told us that having arrived at Omarska railway station you then went to Lamovita. What was the reason for going to Lamovita?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went to a friend of ours, actually a former waiter of Dusko's, who was living there. We did not have transportation, and that part of the road towards Kozarac was not very recommendable and so there was not much traffic going on it. So we went to this Timarac and asked him to give us a ride to Kozarac in his vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you then go with him to the town of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He told us that he did not have enough fuel to take us there, but that he would otherwise. So we went to Lamovita, but let me tell you right away, Lamovita, there was a gas station and there were some structures there, and there was a military unit that was stationed there. The house belonging to Timarac was towards Kozarac, maybe a kilometre or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you get fuel for the car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They gave us a certificate. I think we got 10 litres. Then we tanked fuel and returned to Timarac's house and then we went in his car by the old road, not the asphalt road, to Kozarac, to our family house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: By the "old road" do you mean the old road that would take you from Kozarac to Banja Luka ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: --- which runs for large sections almost parallel to the new highway?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At what time did you arrive in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometime in the afternoon around -- it was the afternoon. I remember that that day there was a funeral in the village, a man died or was killed, I do not know, so we waited for that to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you go to the family home in Marsala Tita Street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What was the state of the home when you visited it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusko's cafe was -- all the windows were smashed, the house, the front of it. My section of it was hit by a shell where I had made the store front and so part of the wall was hit and that store front, that window.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You have told us about the delivery you had had on 21st May. Were those goods still in your store?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Had anything been taken from the store?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe several crates of beer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What about from your brother's cafe, had anything, so far as both of you could tell, been taken from there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that moment, no. Maybe some of the supplies like glasses, but the first time we arrived there the coffee machine was there and it was there on top of the bar where it used to be originally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How long did you stay at the house on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: An hour and a half, approximately, between an hour and hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did the man Timarac remain with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So what did you do at the house at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I entered into my part and Dusko went upstairs and looked around his property. As the shell fell, a portion of those crates were broken and then there were pot marks in the wall, and I had also a number of empty crates because the Banja Luka brewery did not allow me to get a large shipment of, let us say, 1,000 crates at a time. So I could only get 300 or 400 at a time. So I was saving the empty crates. So all this was moved, so from the outside you could see that there was beer in there. I took down the sign where it said "Banja Luka brewery". Then I moved the full crates with beer, because my premises had -- are two parts so there is a partition wall between them. So I moved it to the side so that it would not be seen, and around it I put all those empty crates so that if somebody entered that they would think that it is all empty and they would not take anything. After that I came out and a soldier came, and he got into Pile's car and maybe he wanted to get something out of it or something and Pile ran over and said: "This is mine", and so he got out. Then another one came and he was a tank driver. Then I met him. Dusko was there and Pile.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Who is Pile?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Timarac, Timarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is his nickname, "Pile"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is his nickname; even now everybody calls him "Pile". So I re-entered my premises. I got out four bottles of beer and we came to Dusko's place, stood at the bar. We drank the beer. We asked him to watch, keep an eye on this, because his unit was stationed there. We got into Pile's car and started back to his village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: During this time had your brother Dusko, like you, remained in the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You returned to Lamovita where Timarac lived. Can you tell us what time you arrived there on this day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will tell you, but I just want to add something that I omitted. Before this soldier arrived when we drank the beer, for a while we stood in front of the house for a while. You could not believe that everything was so destroyed, so we were standing around, and a large truck appeared -- a Barava make -- and it came to a stop down from our house. There was a house of Ankic Salih and then there was a building, and so there this truck came and came to a stop when they saw us. There was a kind of a stocky man -- I think he was a sergeant -- and when he got out of the car he pulled out a handgun -- it was a Magnum 357 -- and he pointed it at me. We were all in civilian clothes. He asked us who we were, and I said that I was the owner of the house there, and he looked at us kind of strangely. Then I told him that we were Serbs, because people outside of Kozarac, many people outside of Kozarac, thought that in Kozarac -- maybe somebody did not even know that there were any Serbs living in Kozarac. So he asked us for our IDs. I showed him my personal ID. He told me that we must not move around there in civilian clothes because we could be harmed because people may not know who we were. Then I said that we were going. Then he went into that building, and we got into the car and went to the village of Timarac, to his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What time, if you can tell us, was it that you got back to Lamovita?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was 5.00 or 6 o'clock maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At Lamovita, what did you do then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We came to Pile's house. Before that, Pile -- Dusko got from the attic of our house a hunting gun which belonged to Mladen Tadic and he left it there before the war in the house, and he also took with him an automatic rifle which we brought along together with this hunting rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You have told us about the hunting rifle, but the automatic rifle, do you know how your brother got that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know because he got that automatic rifle even before, before the conflict. I cannot say exactly when, the date, I do not know the date, but I used to see it when I would come to Kozarac. That is, I knew that Dusko at night is keeping watch on the balcony in front of the house or in the cafe during that period of time of the conflict and before the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know where he got that automatic rifle from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He got it from a young man who was in the war in Slavonia and who deserted the unit. He was married to a Muslim woman and a man who did not want to be involved in the war. He did not know how to get rid of the weapon. If he took the weapon to Prijedor, the military police would arrest him because he left his unit. Then he asked Dusko if he could leave the rifle with him and that maybe he could return it somehow, I do not know. He himself did not dare do it, and return it. I think his name was Kusuta.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did he live near Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He lived in a village of Balte, that is, in the vicinity of Kozarac, a few kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Those two weapons then were taken by your brother from the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the attic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Did he take them then away from the house and did you take them with you to Lamovita?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You referred to your brother keeping watch. Had there been any trouble or incidents of trouble at his cafe before the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes. I cannot exactly say the date, one cannot remember everything, but in that period of time when he opened the cafe it was a nice -- very nicely appointed inside. There was a video recorder there. I think there was, I do not know which make, Fisher or Teac. But on one occasion somebody smashed the windows and they took the TV and nobody ever found out who it was, when it was. It was in the early morning hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: From Lamovita did you take those weapons with you and return to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The hunting gun we left. It could not be used. I had not seen such a hunting rifle before. The mechanism was that you had to pull out a pin before you fired. I had never seen it. That hunting gun, when he kept it in the house, he would leave it. He would pull out that part and he would keep it separate in the armoire. When he hid it there, apparently, that trigger mechanism was left in the armoire, so when the conflict in Kozarac came somebody stole that because many things were also stolen. So that at that point it was like nothing, like a stick. We did not take it, so we only brought the automatic rifle with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So was the hunting rifle left with Timarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: From Lamovita how did you return to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We got down to the crossroads of the Prijedor/Banja Luka/Lamovita/Omarska road and there were some police there, there were military. So we hitchhiked and we got a ride on a truck to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What time did you return to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was already towards dusk.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That automatic rifle was taken by your brother back to Banja Luka with him, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was carrying it because he did not have a permit for it and I had -- I have a blank document and I entered the number of the rifle because I had a permit to carry automatic weapons from that Territorial Defence Unit of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You told us that there was a second visit to Kozarac in this period of time. When did that take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think -- actually I know for sure that Dusko went there on another occasion, but not to Kozarac. He went to -- he came to our house, in fact, to the house of my mother-in-law of Jovo Samardzija and at that time Dusko and myself and our mother were at my relatives' there, and I remember him asking if he could -- if somebody or someone of us could go with him to Trnopolje because he found out that his own sister together with the Muslims from Jakupovici, which is where her house was, and Jovo's summer house, that she went together with her neighbours from there to this collection centre in Trnopolje, because there was a possibility that she could be attacked. So, she went alongside with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you go to Trnopolje with Samardzija and your brother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I had some obligations so I could not go but also, let me tell you, I heard that there were all people from Kozarac there so I was not feeling comfortable going there because they were all my neighbours, our neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you have many Muslim friends, Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very many before the war, during the war. In the Unit where I was there were over 100 Muslims, however improbable that may sound. In a Unit where I was there were a lot of Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What I asked you about was the second visit to Kozarac. Can you tell me when that took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The exact date I cannot say, but it was after Dusko's and Jovo's departure for Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You were mobilized on 16th June, as you have told us. Can you tell us what sort of time period before that date this visit would have happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To Kozarac, the second visit to Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, that is the one I am asking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: On this occasion how did you travel to Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went by train to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Who went?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Myself and Dusko.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Again can you tell us what time you would have left Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We left in the afternoon by train. I do not know exactly the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How did you get from Omarska to Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We first arrived also by foot from Omarska to Timarac, to his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you have a ride with him again to Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So how did you get from Lamovita to Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That day we spent at Timarac because it was already late. We spent the night there. Then we asked him to take us to Omarska so that we could find a truck so that I could take my beer to Banja Luka, and Dusko, some of his effects from the cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What was the reason for this second visit that you were now engaged upon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I saw that everything was being taken away, that it was being robbed and plundered, then I thought that our house would not be spared either. So, I simply wanted to evacuate everything, to rescue what I could. It did not matter whether it was a Serb house or a Muslim house, people were just taking and pillaging.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So how many days after the first visit was this second visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Seven or eight days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Having seen Timarac and planned to go to Omarska to get a truck, did Timarac take you to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, to the centre of Omarska. We found a man, a truck, and a young man -- I do not know him, he knew him -- blond, tall. He did not say right away how much he was going to charge us for transportation, but he agreed to bring us some things. He did not know what it was but he said that he would.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was this man your contact, Dusko's contact or a contact of the man Timarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think that he knew him very well in particular, but there were a number of men with the trucks and he was in uniforms and he said: "Would you take us there? We will pay you", and he said he would.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was this a civilian truck or a military truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Whereabouts in Omarska did you find this man with the truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the centre. I do not know Omarska very well. So to the left there was a road and there, there was a truck there. I think it was a Zastava make.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is this near the marketplace?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somewhere around there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did he agree to take you to Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you and your brother go with him back to the family home in Marsala Tita Street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What time on that day would you have returned back to the family home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could have been between 11.00 and 12.00, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This was a few days after your first visit. Had any more possessions from the house been taken during the intervening period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until then I did not know, but when I got there there was not a single crate of beer there. The empty crates had been overturned. The partition that I put in front, that was torn and lying on the floor. From Dusko's cafe they were missing the coffee-making machine and the contraption for tap beer. There was nothing of all the glassware, bottles, the glasses where you poured. It was an empty bar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What about in the family home in the rooms where family members used to live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were some things at that time. It had not been taken away, all of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But had some things been taken away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not living up there so that I could observe that if something had been taken, maybe a refrigerator or something, but as far as the sofa and the armoires, that was there, but things were .....

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So what did you do when you arrived there at the home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We loaded those, some of those empty crates. We took down the top of the bar. It was an aluminium construction, that is how it was made, so we took that whole thing down. That was just above the bar, and we took down -- it was on hooks. They were light and they were part of the decorations, so we took that down as well. So that was it. I think we also brought -- there was a heavy marble table top. We loaded that in and after that we went back to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So you loaded these things into the truck. Did you have a full load or a part load?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So-so. There were more empty crates than things really.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What time did you leave Kozarac on this visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 4 o'clock, 3 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did the man who owned the lorry drive you and your brother back to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What happened then when you arrived at Banja Luka with the lorry, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He drove those things to Koste Jarica Street, the house that Dusko and his children were living in and his mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were they off loaded there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and we put those things -- Dusko was living in the basement and when you enter the yard there was a wooden door and we opened it from the inside, so we put those things upstairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How long did ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But not all of them. I am sorry, not all of them, just Dusko's things. My things were unloaded at my mother-in-law's because I had a shop there before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How long did those things remain at that house in Koste Jarica Street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusko's things remained a month maybe, maybe even two months, after Dusko's departure from Banja Luka or, rather, from Prijedor and Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You have told us that your brother was mobilized on 16th June. Where was he working from 16th June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusko, as I said, was assigned to the traffic police and he worked at a checkpoint at Orlovci which is a few kilometres from Prijedor in the direction of Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So was that with the Prijedor police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When he went to work for the Prijedor police, did his family remain in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did they ever move to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you tell us if you know when that would have been?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly, but roughly it was 15 or 20 days when they moved out completely, 15 or 20 days after Dusko started working, maybe 15 days, after Dusko started working in the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
