utterances.text: You told us that you were mobilized on 16th June. Where were you stationed initially from that date of 16th June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After June 16th nothing changed in my unit. Actually, the Territorial Defence Unit was transformed into the 2nd Light Infantry Brigade of Banja Luka. There were several such Light Infantry Brigades formed in the territory of Starcevici, Mejdan and Ada -- these are districts of the town -- and from then the 2nd Light Infantry Brigade was formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So did you remain then in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How long did you remain in Banja Luka during your period of mobilization?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until 6th or 7th July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In that period that your brother started his mobilization in Prijedor from 16th June until the family left for Prijedor some 20 days later, did you see your brother in Banja Luka? Did he return to visit the family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you tell us on how many occasions, if you know, that would have been?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Several times and he would come and visit me too, because we were all close.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your mobilization in Banja Luka at that time, did that mean that you lived in the barracks or did you live in your usual house or apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The command headquarters was in Kastel. This is a part of town in the centre. There was a building there. There were two restaurants and one of the buildings in which the command was based, half of it was the command and the other half was a carpet shop, a wholesale store.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But did you sleep there or did you sleep back at your home? Did you have a pass or a discharge that enabled you to be elsewhere than in the base of the Unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not assigned to the Kastel, the barracks. I continued to be performing the same duty as before when I was part of the Territorial Defence and I slept at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: During this period until that date in July when you moved from Banja Luka, did you ever visit your brother in Prijedor or the family in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not move anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, I was asking whether you visited your brother in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Unit being based in Banja Luka, did it remain in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, not all the time. A part of the Unit, about 20 men from our Unit and 20 men from the 2nd Light, the 4th Light, roughly, more than 20, maybe 40 to 50 people from my Unit, were sent to Vlasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About the 6th or 7th July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you go to Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So was that on 6th or 7th July that you went to Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 6th or 7th, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In that period from when your brother moved to Prijedor to work from 16th June until you yourself went to Vlasic on 6th or 7th July, on how many occasions did you visit him or the family in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were they just day visits or did you stay for any period overnight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once I spent the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You have told us that you were mobilized within the 2nd Light Infantry and that you, amongst others, went to Vlasic. How long did you serve at Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly the date, but I know that I returned for maybe five days before the 26th of -- just a moment please -- I went on 6th or 7th July and I was there until -- I am sorry, I must try and remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you have a younger son born at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And what was the date of his birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was born on 26th August.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So, did you come back for his birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I returned before he was born.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you tell us about how many days or the exact number of days, if you can, before he was born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Four or five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So what were you doing at Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My Unit was located at Vitovlje, a part of Vlasic, there was a school there, and I was stationed at a part called Kajin Kamen. It is a left of a unit from Celinac which was stationed just across Dobrotici, a village which was mostly inhabited by Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If you can give us an indication, about how far from Travnik was the place that you were based?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could have been six to 10 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What was ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Can you give us any indication of where in Yugoslavia Vlasic is?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have actually asked for a map that shows this area. Unfortunately, I have been unsuccessful. Maybe over the luncheon adjournment the Prosecution, who I am sure would probably have a map of this particular area, could help us. Thank you. [To the witness]: At this time what was your Unit concerned with? What were you doing there at Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know for sure at that time operations had started in the city of Jajce, and our assignment or the assignment of a part of our Unit and these other units was to prevent the breakthrough of those units towards Vitovlje towards the relay station to prevent its capture.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: These were your orders, were they, as part of your mobilization that you had to spend this period at Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You served there for this period of time. After the birth of your son did you return to Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: During this time that you served at Vlasic did you ever see any convoys of refugees travelling to Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had no personal contact with them, but I saw them in passing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you see or come across any attacks or did you take part in yourself any attacks on those convoys involving refugees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you see any attacks on those convoys?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Having served there during this period of time and returning to Banja Luka, did you return to your Unit or were you given leave of absence for a period of time from the Unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I returned to Banja Luka. I was given about 15 days leave of absence because of the birth of my son and I was in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you tell us when it was that you rejoined your Unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around the second half of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In that period of 15 days did you visit your brother or see your brother during this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Where was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I first went to Prijedor to visit them and to inform them of the happy news that I had a third son.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did your brother Dusko visit you in Banja Luka at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my mother came, his wife and Dusko. They came during the day and went back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was that to see the new baby?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you returned to your Unit after this 15 days of absence, did you resume duties in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For a few days, yes, and then I was told in the headquarters that they wanted to fill in a military police squad belonging to the 2nd Infantry Brigade, and they asked me whether I wanted to be transferred to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you transferred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was not a transfer really. It was the same Unit, only I was no longer in the Starcevica Detachment, as it was called in that part of town, but I was in the military police of the 2nd Light Infantry Brigade and the same military postal code.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did your duties keep you within Banja Luka or did you have to serve elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The duties of the military police, these were Brigade Military Police because the Corps Military Police had much higher authorizations. The Brigade Police only had authority over its Unit if something were to happen within our Unit. If somebody was to desert or something it was our duty to catch him and bring him back. That was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was this in Banja Luka or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So this period of service, did that require you to live in barracks in Banja Luka or were you able to live at your usual home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it is nearby. It was in the centre of the city. It was not a barracks. It was a building, as part of Kastel, a part of the old city where there was a building, a shed, and inside were the offices of the Police Commander, the person on duty and a large room with about 10 beds.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How long did you remain within the military police of your Unit, the Brigade Military Police, in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed throughout until I was transferred to a completely different unit until '94, but our Unit afterwards was relocated to another location. The whole Unit went to Donji Svilaj. It is somewhere near Bosanski Brod.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When were you finally demobilized from the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On Women's Day, March 8th 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So in the period from 1994 when you were transferred yet again to 1996 where did you serve?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spent a part of the time -- I must tell you that in September I was in Banja Luka. Then in October I was also there. At the end of October my Unit went to Donji Svilaj and the Commander went with them, but because the administration stayed behind in Banja Luka then they needed to select four policemen who would stay in Banja Luka to provide security for the people who had stayed behind, and also if somebody were to desert they would let us know and we would have to bring them back to Svilaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are you talking about 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What I asked about was 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In January of 1994, or to be more precise in November, I had some problems with my wife. She fell ill. These were the consequences of her delivery, two months after the delivery, and she lost a great deal of weight. From 70 something her weight dropped to 45. So she had serious health problems. So I was among one of those people who stayed on in Banja Luka. They showed understanding for me and I stayed on. In the meantime I met several colleagues who offered the possibility for me to join another unit in Banja Luka. It was not so easy in those days to move from one unit to another. So I did not. I went to Svilaj for two shifts of 10 days each. The Commander, I told him about my problems and then I stayed. After, when she recovered, after the New Year, I went for these two shifts. In the meantime my Unit, there was talk of it entering the Doboj zone of responsibility. I was in Doboj until the beginning of '94. So I am giving you the whole account of where I was. In December of '93 I was offered the possibility, some friends of mine who had trained with me were accompanying the Lieutenant Colonel Borivoje Pavlovic in TG1 Jasenovac. This belonged to Jas Krajina, but some Units from the Banja Luka Corps were located there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Going back to 1992, in that period from September until the end of the year did you ever return to visit Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: About what sort of frequency would that have been during that period from September until the end of the year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe four or five times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you meet your brother in Kozarac on those occasions when you visited?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know what he was doing in Kozarac at that time when you visited him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then the police station had been formed in Kozarac, the Local Commune, and he was there in the police, he and Bosko Dragicevic, Zivco, I forget the surname, an older man, I will remember probably, and some others. He worked in the Local Commune. These were activities regarding resettlement of people, the revival of life in Kozarac. He was active in the Red Cross. I saw him distributing relief, he and Branka Jasikovic, Danijela and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: During this period during your visits, were they short visits or did you spend some time in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Several hours at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What were you doing there? Why had you visited the place at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Simply because I wanted to see the place and my brother. That is why.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, we will stand in recess for lunch until 2.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Over the luncheon adjournment we had some maps provided to us by the Prosecution and I tender these before the Court as Exhibit D81, I think it is -- 88, is it? There are three copies for the Court and I understand there is no objection. If one could be put in front of the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection, Miss Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: D88 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we call that D88A, in fact, it might assist because there is one copy of a full scale map which shows the general area which might assist the Court. We have both agreed that it would be helpful if you had this full scale map for yourselves. So if I submit that now as 88B and it is in colour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection to 88B?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Defence 88A -- we will mark it -- and 88B then are admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Mr. Tadic, we have here a map showing the Vlasic region which is to the south of the map. Can you see Travnik at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is it correct that highlighted in yellow is Paljenik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says "Paljenik".

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: "Paljenik". That, apparently, is the top of the mountain, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We can see Banja Luka in the middle of this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There is a road that goes down from Banja Luka near Radici through Skender Vakuf, Donji Karicani, Vitovlje, joining the main road fairly close to Travnik at a place called Turbe, is that right, leaving the Banja Luka road at Jagare?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If you can perhaps identify for us again where it was that you were stationed when you were on Vlasic Mountain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We came to Vitovlje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Vitovlje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the direction of Skender Vakuf towards Vitovlje. That is where we went.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was your Unit stationed at any particular base near Vitovlje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in the settlement of Vitovlje. We were there for several days in the school building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that the only place where you were stationed or did you also move from there elsewhere on Vlasic mountain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They directed us to Kajin Kamen. That is what that part of it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Kajin Kamen, can you tell us where that is in relation to Vitovlje and Paljenik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The line here, there is a point and then Vitovlje towards Paljenic, but still more towards No. 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I see. We can see just above Kosici, the figure 13.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in that area, just above Vitovlje, that is also where the village Dobrotici is, but it is not on the map. It is not written.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I do not think this is terribly important, is it? We did have testimony weeks ago about Travnik, but unless it relates to that, I do not -- we are now in 1994, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, 1992, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 1992, excuse me. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Anyway, that is all I ask. I have concluded my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Cross-examination, Miss Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, your father was a well-known and respected man in Kozarac, was he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In fact, when your father died everyone in Kozarac came to the funeral?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, a lot of people were at the funeral, and I think that about 99 per cent of all people of Kozarac did show up at the funeral.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your mother was also a well-known and respected woman in the community, was she not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your house was on the main street, the main business street, of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Marsala Tita Street, No. 36.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Because of your mother and father, in large part, the Tadic family was very well known in Kozarac, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your brother Dusko Tadic was well known in Kozarac because of his karate activities, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not only because of that.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: For what other things was he well known in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had a cafe and he also lived in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: He was very well known as a very accomplished sportsman, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You could say so.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: He had a karate club or class and often had, perhaps, even 90 students at a time, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had classes of karate and also he had registered a club which was called Borac in Kozarac, but it was a chain. I also had one by the same name but in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Many of his students in these karate classes were Muslim men, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I believe you testified that your brother opened his cafe in Kozarac at the end of 1990 or perhaps the beginning of 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: His cafe in Kozarac was a very popular place, I believe you testified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the younger people mostly.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: After your brother supposedly received this threatening letter, your brother and his family did not leave Kozarac, did they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: They were not killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Instead, some short time later he opened this popular cafe of his, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he had already been preparing these materials to open it up.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You testified that you yourself were not interested in politics and you thought politics could even be dangerous, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The SDS was a political party, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a movement and then it turned into a party. That is how I see it.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: It was a party that advocated Serb unity and a common state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably, but I was not taking part in the activities of that party.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You were not aware that the SDS advocated Serb unity and a common state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that, but I did not participate in the activities of the party.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the time period when these parties were being established and when Milosevic became a very popular person, a very popular politician?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall during that time period that pictures of him could be seen all over Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic was perceived as someone who stood up for the desire of Serbs to be united, is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You could say so.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic also made it clear that Serbs were really one people and that national or republic borders could not separate them, is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: During this time period many Serbs were naming their newly born sons after Milosevic, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is possible, but I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you or your brother Dusko consider naming any of your children after Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It never crossed my mind.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: During this same time period Serbs began to wear what could be considered nationalist symbols such as two headed eagles, did they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What period of time?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: During this period of time when nationalism was becoming more of an issue, Mr. Milosevic was becoming more popular?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, many of them did.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Many of them to show their Serb identity also began to wear symbols of the Orthodox church, did they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the same as Muslims wore symbols of Islam and Croats Croat symbols. So certain Serbs who were more nationalist and orientation, they wore Serbian insignia.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: During your testimony you have talked about certain dates and times in 1992. I would like to go back to some of those. In April 1992 did your brother Dusko accompany you when you took Mira Tadic and the family to the village of Kozice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: On 29th April did you drive to Kozice to pick up Mira Tadic and the family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you have any personal knowledge of how Mira Tadic and the family made their way from Kozice back to Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did Mira Tadic and the family go with you when you went to Kozarac on 1st May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I believe you testified that, to your recollection, your brother Dusko and his family came to your home on 3rd or 4th May 1992, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did your brother and his family remain in your home on 3rd, 4th, 5th and 6th May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: To your recollection, did Dusko and his family remain with you in your home in Banja Luka on 3rd, 4th, 5th and 6th May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: It was after that that they moved to this house on Koste Jarica Street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was near my apartment, and during those days they were going there to prepare the house so that they could move in there. All the works around the renovations were done by a friend of mine, Hamdija Besirevic. He is a Muslim and he is a house painter and so he did that.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: This is the house on Koste Jarica Street that we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You said that they lived in the basement of that house. When you say the "basement" do you mean that they lived in the ground floor area or did they live in rooms that were actually below ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Below the ground, looking from the front of the building, of the house, from the street.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: As you came around to the back to enter into the area where they lived, was that level with the ground at that point or did you actually have to go down below the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You turn around the house, there is a concrete and then you enter into those rooms there.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So those are on the ground level in the back of the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You spoke of the blockade of Kozarac beginning, I believe you said, on 22nd May. Is that your memory of when that began?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You were not in Kozarac on 23rd May, were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was on 21st.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Right. You were not there on 22nd May, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not go into Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You were not in Kozarac on 23rd, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, on 22nd nobody could enter Kozarac and it was difficult to get out too because on the one side it was blocked by the Serbian military and the police and on the inside by the Muslim units, by the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You heard that from whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was seeing those checkpoints even earlier when I was coming there, they existed, from the direction of Prijedor at the entrance of Kozarac, also when you leave, where Mrakovica and towards Kozarusa and towards Banja Luka by the old road in Kamicani.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: These various checkpoints that you are talking about, who were manning these checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Muslim young men who were the members of the Territorial Defence of BH, they had insignia with the army BH on it.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where were the Serb checkpoints located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serbian checkpoint was in Orlovci, but the point from Banja Luka was still not there at the time. It was only around the 22nd.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So, prior to 22nd when you were travelling to Kozarac you also travelled to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 21st it was the last time that I was in Kozarac, but I did not go to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: On prior visits to Kozarac in April and May 1992, did you go to Prijedor on any of those visits?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: On 23rd May you did not travel with your brother from Kozarac to Banja Luka, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You did not meet him upon his arrival in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You met him when he first arrived or he came to your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When he arrived he stopped over at my place, and then went up to his family, because as you come into Banja Luka first you come to my apartment and then Milosa Duica Street, Koste Jarica Street, where he was.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So he came to your house at some point after his arrival ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To my apartment.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: --- in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall what time it was that he came to your house on 23rd May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometime in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall how long he stayed with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A very short period of time.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you began performing your TO duties, I believe you said it was in April 1992, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 5th April.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who was it who contacted you and told you that you were obligated to perform these duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked in Cajavec before that and I was in the civilian defence. When I stopped working I could not be attached to the Cajavec any more. I had to report to one of those Local Communes, because there was a person in charge of the military affairs within every company.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So who was it who actually informed you that you had to report for TO duties in April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the one person in charge in the Cajavec, he told me that when you leave the company you had to turn in everything. There was a uniform with a hat and a jacket, and you had to turn it in. When I turned it in he said: "You have to report to the civilian defence, not to the Local Commune, and you will belong to the Territorial Defence", which is also the civilian defence.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So you turned your uniform and all of your equipment in to your company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What uniform and equipment did you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: For your company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A blue uniform, which insignia, it is the civilian defence and a blue jacket and shoes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you reported to the Local Commune, do you remember the position of the person to whom you reported?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was in charge of the Territorial Defence of the Local Commune Starcevici. His name was Vaso Grozdanic.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: At that time you were now again issued a uniform and equipment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you at any time during your TO service issued a uniform and equipment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you were issued this uniform, what kind of uniform were you issued?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A camouflage uniform, it was.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you say a "camouflage uniform", what colours were in this camouflage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Similar to like NATO is wearing, but they were multi-coloured. They were camouflage uniforms, and that uniform I did not get from the TO Unit, but myself and this Vaso Grozdanic went to the director of the company called Vitaminka, because there was a problem with uniforms. Not all soldiers had uniforms. They were old JNA uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: But this company had these camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they invoiced 10 uniforms through this company that was making military uniforms. So I got one, he got another one and others got others.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Again this camouflage uniform would have been one that had browns, blacks and greens in it, are they the colours that we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not say there were black, they were greens, there were all kinds of colours, but less of the black.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you also get a hat with this uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you get all with the uniform, a hat also.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The hat was also camouflage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What kind of weapon were you issued for your duties with the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you receive ammunition as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How much ammunition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A complete charge of four and the fifth cartridge was in the rifle itself with also the cleaning supplies.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I am not quite sure I understand. How many bullets did you actually receive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Four cartridges by 30 bullets, so that is 120, and fifth was another 30, so in total 150 bullets.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your job while you were in the TO was to protect certain buildings in Banja Luka, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Those buildings included Orthodox church, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did those buildings also include the mosques that were in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the part where I was, where my Unit was stationed, there were no mosques.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you know if other TO units in Banja Luka had the job of protecting the mosques there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, probably, but I think that they did not preserve them very well. If they did, they did not protect them very well.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: They were all destroyed, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When was it, do you recall the date, that you were actually issued with your weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I signed for the weapon several days after I joined the Territorial Defence Unit, so it could have been 7th or 10th April.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How much later did you actually get your uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe it was about 10 days, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: On the 23rd May did you meet with any of the Muslims who supposedly left Kozarac and came to Banja Luka on that date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not on the 23rd, but it could have been 25th, 6th, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us the names of those people that you met with, those Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Adem Kahrimanovic, I saw him personally and I sat down with him and drank coffee. We talked, so .....

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you know where Mr. Kahrimanovic is today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard that he is in Austria.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you. From 23rd May onwards, while the attack continued in Kozarac, were you with your brother Dusko every hour of every day that he was in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 23rd, it was not the date of the attack on Kozarac; it was 24th, it was a Sunday.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: During the days, the several days, that this attack on Kozarac lasted were you with your brother every hour of every one of those days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you with your brother every hour of every evening during those days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not all the time.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you actually spend the night with him every night when he slept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You talked about a first visit that you made to Kozarac. I believe you indicated that on that visit you and your brother walked on the road from the Omarska train station to Lamovita, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What would be the distance that you would have walked from the train station to Lamovita?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately three kilometres, four.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: During that walk from the train station to Lamovita, did you ever have to show your papers to any police or military along that route?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I believe you indicated that there were soldiers in Lamovita?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were everywhere. It was in Omarska, in the town and also in Lamovita -- I mean, in the town of Omarska and also a unit was also located in Lamovita.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What unit was it that was located in Lamovita, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know which unit it was, but it was a unit from that area.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: These soldiers that you saw all over in Omarska and in Lamovita, what kind of uniforms were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some had camouflage, some had old Yugoslav, some had none and had weapons. So that is how it was.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you say the "old Yugoslav" uniform, you are talking about what is referred to as the SMB uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What kind of weapons did these people that you saw in uniform have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some had PAP rifle, semi-automatic, some automatic with wooden butt, some with the ones that can be disassembled, so different ones.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you say a "PAP rifle", do you mean PAP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A semi-automatic, polu automatska puska, PAP.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you were in Lamovita, did you or your brother have to show your papers to any of the soldiers in Lamovita?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not right away. We did not go to that unit in Lamovita right away. We went to a young man who worked at Dusko's as a waiter. We went to his house.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you went to get the gas certificate, is that when you went to the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who was it who actually gave you this gas certificate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not issued for me, but somebody gave it to Dusko. He was probably a uniformed officer, the responsible person who was there. I did not know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When this person gave the gas certificate to Dusko, during this transaction were either you or your brother required to show your papers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said that he would have to go to see his family there and he was approved 10 litres of petrol for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who said he would have to go see his family? Are you talking about your brother Dusko said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, not his family, his family home.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you were in Kozarac that day you talked about seeing a tank driver there and having a beer with that tank driver?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I said I saw a tank at the entrance to Kozarac. I saw a tank driver, a blond man called -- his name was Milan Vlacina. I did not know his name at the time, but we were introduced. He actually came up to our family home when we passed, when we reached the house, and then he came up to us.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who introduced him to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He came alone. I think that Dusko did not know him either. I am not sure that this man knew him either, but he was a soldier of the Republika Srpska. One could see immediately that he was a soldier and he stated his name. So we exchanged a few words. I went into my part of the house, my business premises. Before he came, I saw that a shell had fallen on my part of this premise, of the business, and part of the packaging and the crates. So a lot of them were thrown around in front, some were mine, some belonging to other people probably. There were these crates. So I moved them to the left, so as to cover them. When he came I brought four beers and we had them in Dusko's cafe at the bar.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What kind of a uniform was this man Vlacina wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was the old Yugoslav uniform.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you know a woman named Nada Vlacina, a friend of your brother Dusko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I met them when Dusko was moving to Prijedor. When I came to visit Dusko in his flat I met her then.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you ever meet her husband?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That man was her husband.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The man in Kozarac was her husband?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: On this first visit to Kozarac when you left Lamovita that day, I believe you said that you went to the crossroads for Lamovita and the Prijedor/Banja Luka road and there were some police at that crossroads?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were army people, there was the police, there were both military men and policemen at the crossroads there.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did these policemen, whether they were military or civilian police, ask to see your papers or Dusko's papers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because this man called Pile Timarac was with us. He drove us to this crossroads. They probably knew him and probably those people came from that same unit. When we were looking for the fuel, they knew us, simply nobody asked for anything, and so we stopped a lorry and we went to Banja Luka with it.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So at that time Pile Timarac was also in the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he came from Sisak or somewhere like that. I do not know whether he was a soldier before that, but then he had not been mobilized either because he was not wearing a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: On this first occasion when you and your brother went to Kozarac, what were you and your brother wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Civilian clothes, jeans and a jacket, the first time I went.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your brother was not wearing a uniform on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You have mentioned Pile Timarac several times. What is his proper first name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Timarac -- I knew, but I have forgotten it -- Milenko, I think it was, Milenko Timarac, but we had a problem that day in Kozarac when we got there. Before this Milan Vlacina came up, a large truck appeared and stopped there; and as we were standing in front of the house, a little lower down near the barber's shop, maybe five, 10 metres lower down, a soldier, a heavily built man -- I think he had a sergeant insignia -- and he pointed a rifle at me and he asked who we were and what we were looking for. I said that this was our house, our family house. He looked at us strangely and then I said: "We are Serbs". He wanted our papers. I showed him my ID card and he said: "What are you looking for here? Get away. You must not roam around in civilian clothes. You could get killed". So I said: "All right", and we got into the car and left.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So you got into the car and you went back then to Lamovita? So it was after this first visit in Kozarac that you then went back to Lamovita and from there then you returned to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You did this all in the same day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, during the time period of May, June and July 1992, how many different kinds of uniforms did your brother Dusko have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Certainly. To your knowledge, during the time period of May, June and July 1992, how many different kinds of uniforms did your brother Dusko have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what those uniforms looked like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first uniform was when we went to Kozarac the second time I was wearing my uniform, and Dusko was wearing a camouflage uniform, a summer camouflage uniform. It was not a real uniform actually, but camouflage clothes that are worn over uniforms which I had given him. It could not be used as a uniform. You could wear it on top of your uniform. It had a hood. It was brown, spotted, with spots.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You had given him this uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall when it was that you gave him this uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before leaving for Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what year or what month that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second time we went to Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So it was in what month of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: June, the month of June.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So you gave him that uniform at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was the other kind of uniform that your brother had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Another time I saw him wearing a uniform, it was a policeman's uniform. That was when he was mobilized for the reserve police force of Prijedor. It was a classical uniform of the traffic police.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You said on your second visit to Kozarac that you and your brother were both wearing a uniform; your brother wearing this uniform you had given him. What kind of uniform were you wearing on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had, I think it was, some kind of a camouflage uniform. It was a camouflage uniform. The camouflage uniform I received, as I said, from the company. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Thank you. Now on the first time that you went to Kozarac, were you carrying any weapons with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had a personal pistol, my own personal property. It was left by my father, 765, as a token of remembrance.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What kind of weapon did your brother take with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did not have any weapon.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: On this second visit to Kozarac, what kind of weapon did you take with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I took an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What kind of weapon did your brother take with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I believe you said it was the second occasion when you loaded up some things in a truck and then actually drove in the truck back from Kozarac to Banja Luka, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I omitted to mention that the first time we were there Dusko from the loft of our family house took down a hunting rifle and an automatic rifle, and we took that to Lamovita. We left the hunting rifle with Pile and we took with us the automatic rifle. That was the first time. The second time we went with weapons. We got to Omarska and we looked for a lorry for me and him to transport our things to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You went back from Kozarac to Banja Luka in this truck, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: On your return trip from Kozarac to Banja Luka, were you stopped anywhere along the road to be checked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no one stopped us because the driver was wearing a uniform. He was from Omarska. People knew him and we too were wearing uniforms, so no one stopped us.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You have talked about how your brother acquired this automatic weapon. Is it your testimony that you were present when this young man supposedly gave the weapon to your brother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So you were not present when that event supposedly ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not present, but I gave him a licence for that rifle so that nobody would take it away from him.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you see your brother Dusko Tadic the day that he went to Trnopolje with Jovo Samardzija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: On the day that he went to Trnopolje with Jovo Samardzija what was your brother wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: On that date did he have a weapon with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him and I cannot say whether he had a weapon because I do not know. They did not go that very moment because Jovo Samardzija's house and the house of my wife's parents is about 50 or 80 metres away from one another, and that is where I saw them because I saw Jovo. Dusko was with me. Jovo came to ask whether one of us would go with him to Trnopolje. I could not. I had other obligations and he asked Dusko. Dusko said: "All right, I will go" and they went. I did not go with them so I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So was it your understanding that they were going to leave directly from where you were and go to the train station to go to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You have talked about the time period when you were mobilized. At that time were you given additional uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you given an additional weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you given any additional cartridges of ammunition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, except what I already said.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You testified that your brother went to Prijedor on 15th June 1992. On that occasion you did not go to Prijedor with him, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that he went on 16th June.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So he did not go on 15th, he went on 16th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Me? Dusko went on 16th of June to Prijedor. That was the day of the general mobilization for all people in the Autonomous Region of Krajina; that was what it was proclaimed as.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: On that date, on 16th, when he went to Prijedor, did you accompany him when he went to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but before that he called from my flat, he called a man asking him to fix it so that he could join up with the reserve traffic police, because he feared that if he went to Prijedor and the place he lived in belonged to Prijedor, so he feared that he would have to join up the 5th Kozara Brigade, which was located in Slavonia. It was a combat unit which was on the front already.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: After 16th June you continued to live in Banja Luka, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You never moved to Prijedor, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In 1992 did you keep any kind of daily calendar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, I did not understand you.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Let us try this again. In 1992 did you keep any type of daily calendar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you keep any type of daily diary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Since these events occurred, have you spoken with anyone to refresh your memory about the dates you have testified to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I remember these things by certain events that are linked to those days. For example, on 29th April everybody knew the Serb militia took over authority in Prijedor. Everyone knew that. So in relation to that date I could remember when I went to Kozarac and things like that, when my son was born. So I knew when I came from Vlasic, I cannot say exactly the day and hour, but in that period these are the events that serve as guidelines.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So, have you spoken with anyone to help refresh your memory about these dates and times you have testified to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Several times I was interviewed by certain TV stations, but they did not ask me ----

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --- about those dates, dates.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So you did not discuss those dates with them?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Why do you not repeat the question so that we can make sure Mr. Tadic heard you?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. You are not hearing anything that is being said, Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No translation. I am hearing French.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Are you getting a translation now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So, you did not speak with any of these television journalists about these dates?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall from what television stations these television journalists were from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could try to remember. The first TV station was Spiegel from Germany.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall when it was that you spoke with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A little after Dusko's arrest, when they came to Banja Luka, they looked me up.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you remember what month and year it was that they came to Banja Luka and looked you up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was February, end of February.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That was what year?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When your brother was arrested in Germany, did you talk to anyone at that time about the dates that you have testified to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but I learnt about his arrest from a friend, a Muslim, who was with me in the unit. He was a Muslim and he was mobilized into the Serb Army. He saw it on television and told me, asking me: "What is this Tadic to you?" I said: "Whom?" and then I said: "He is my brother".

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you talk with your brother about these dates after he was arrested in Germany?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not the dates, but his arrest, yes, and about how it could have happened so. More recently, while he was in prison in Germany I had no contact with him. I could not contact him until he was transferred to The Hague when we were allowed to communicate on the phone. We spoke generally about everything, but not about dates in particular.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So you spoke about the events in the opstina but not about particular dates?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I may have said something, but I cannot remember. Maybe we did mention something, but I cannot recollect.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many times you may have spoken with your brother since he has been here in the prison in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe 10, 20 times.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Have you spoken with Mira Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On Mondays when I had a connection, usually it was Mondays.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Have you spoken with Mira Tadic to help refresh your memory as to these dates you have testified about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Have you spoken to any other Defence witnesses to help refresh yourself about the dates you have testified about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not know many of those people in person. Many people that testified in the case of Dusko Tadic I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You have from time to time been involved with transporting those witnesses to and from various locations in the Banja Luka area, have you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: On how many occasions would you say you have done that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Many, on many occasions.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of any of those Defence witnesses that you have transported back and forth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us some of those names, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When (redacted) returned from The Hague and Mrs. Zorica was with us, so I drove him to Kozarac, because the drivers who had brought them from Belgrade were tired. So I drove them there together with Zorica and then we immediately came back.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall any other names of Defence witnesses that you have transported?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not transport the witnesses when they came to The Hague. This was done by Dragan and Mr. Pietro mostly, in most cases.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Have you read any documents concerning this case to help refresh your memory about dates?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Have you read any witness statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Have you been told about the contents of any witness statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not have the chance to attend the hearing of witnesses that Mr. Wladimiroff conducted, the investigations. I frequently drove them and each time when they spoke to the witnesses they asked me several times actually to move away, not to listen to the investigation. Then I realised that that was the rule, so I would go back to my car and wait.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Have you watched any of the television proceedings of this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Banja Luka one cannot watch the Bosnia-Herzegovina television station. The part of the city that I live in is under a hill, and I think us and our signal, our relay station at Kozara was destroyed by NATO pact raids by Tomahawk rockets so that we can only watch the S channel, that is, the Serb channel in the Republika Srspka. We can watch Zagreb, the first programme some people, second programme as well. At times, in the evenings, when they had a programme, "Slika Na Slika" (Picture Against Picture), these were not telecasts of the trial but just reports that the trial had begun and things like that, but nobody could really tell me precisely what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did these reports ever summarise any of the testimony that had been given?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, and I was disappointed that no one from the Serb television or the media did not want to report anything in connection with Dusko.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you ever told not to watch any of these proceedings on television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, I did not know I would be a witness until recently.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You have testified that while you served in the Vlasic Mountain area that you did not take part in any attacks on convoys of civilians that were going through that area, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You have testified that you never saw any attacks take place on convoys of civilians that were going through that area, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I heard when I was on leave, when I was resting, so there was one day on duty, one day there, so they said that a Commander of one of those units ordered some to turn around. There was a luxury car and people were passing through Mount Vlasic.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So you heard that some vehicles were turned around?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a luxury car. It was a passenger vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is the only thing you ever heard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not the only thing.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you aware that on 17th August a very large convoy came through that area, perhaps 55 cars, maybe as many as 15 trucks, six to eight buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is possible that it was then when they said that it happened that some vehicles were kidnapped, but people were released and sent to Travnik, but I was in Vlasic until 23rd August.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: On 17th August you are not aware that this large convoy containing Muslims and Croats from Sanski Most was stopped and women were taken off the convoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You never heard of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not hear that, but after I went back to Banja Luka I heard that people were taken from Prijedor towards Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So you are not aware that on this date, on 17th August, it was in the Vitovlje area that these women were taken off the bus by Serb soldiers and local Serb men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. Again I repeat, I heard that some luxury cars had been taken and then there were -- it was ordered they be returned, but I said about Kajin Kamen and near Dobrotici, it is a few kilometres from Vitovlje.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You are not aware of the massacre of Muslim men that occurred on the Vlasic Mountain area on 21st August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was up there I did not know, but when I came to Banja Luka I heard about something, but I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You heard about the massacre on 21st August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were talking about that there was something, but I did not know what, apparently, that there was something there and that some young man survived and so he reported on that.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You were aware, were you not, during the time you were in the Vlasic Mountain area that convoys routinely went through with Muslims and Croats who were being expelled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard that for the first time when those cars, apparently, had been taken, and after that I heard more when I came back from Banja Luka to my unit.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: While you were in place you had no idea that civilians, Muslims and Serb civilians, were being forced to leave buses and walk across the confrontation line to freedom? You had no awareness of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not because there was shelling from both sides so there was great fear. There was a shift before me. A young man was slaughtered on the part of Croats and then four young men from Dobrotici had their heads cut off, and then they were calling from the other side: "Send us the others because we can play soccer with their heads. They do not go straight". So we had no experience in combat.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So you knew about this event, but you did not know anything about the civilians who were being forced to cross the confrontation lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I knew about this event in Dobrotici because the unit in which these men were had left their positions and then they were ordered back to those positions.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You have indicated that you have spoken to several TV journalists and you mentioned Spiegel TV as one of those television stations. Do you recall any of the other television stations that you have spoken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I do not know whether it was the BBC, but it is a Madam Pauletta. She was working on a film so she did an interview with all of us, the whole family.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me try to recall. It could have been maybe four or five months ago.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So that would have been late spring or summer of this year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was this year.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What other television stations journalists have you spoken with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just before the opening of the trial there was terrible pressure brought to bear on us. Many TV stations would come and through the press centre they asked to talk to members of the family. We tried to avoid many of them. We did not want to talk about it, knowing what journalists are like, but then we had to talk to some. There was no way of avoiding them. They would come to our house.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you ever go to the Hotel Bosna in Banja Luka and watch television there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I am not working anywhere. I do not -- I really cannot afford to go and have a drink in a restaurant. I am a married man. I have three children. There are five of us and I really cannot afford much entertainment. I went to the Bosna Hotel only when Mr. Wladimiroff and Miss Sylvia came to Banja Luka, to be there, to drive them some place, if necessary, and to give them a hand.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: While you were waiting for them there, did you ever watch television there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, in that part, in the lobby, there was no TV set, and in the piano bar there were mostly spots were being shown via satellite. There was a TV set, but mostly foreign programmes were being screened because they probably had a satellite dish.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you visit your brother Mladen in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I go to Kozarac, but the last three or four months I went when the Defence team would come and I went with them. I would go there. We would say "Hello". I would visit my mother. She does not have a TV set upstairs. Mladen does have one in his business premises. I watched just once briefly the trial. There was a man from Prijedor. I did not know him and he was not talking about Dusko but about some quite different things, and we had to go because we were busy.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You have indicated that you yourself were not interested in politics, but that was not true of your brother, is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I do not think he indicated that. I do not think he said it even in those terms, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe he indicated: "I am not interested in politics. I find them dangerous".

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: He indicated that he cautioned his brother about it because of the experience with his father. I think the objection really goes to the way that you have characterised his testimony suggesting that those words were used.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I simply asked him -- let me try it again, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Rephrase it. I remember. MISS HOLLIS (To the witness): You have indicated that you are not interested in politics. However, that is not true of your brother, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusko Tadic was no politician of any kind. He was a man who at the time sought to assist the Serb people who had come from the Cazin Krajina, who had fled from Bugojno, Jajce and many other places, to settle down, to provide some kind of food for them via the Red Cross. As far as I heard, he was a member of the SDS but he held no position in it. Afterwards, he participated in the revival effort in Kozarac, in the accommodation of these people, in assisting the refugees from Cazin Krajina to survive.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: But is it not true that your brother himself says that he was one of the first members of the SDS in opstina Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To be a member of SDS does not mean to say that one is a politician.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Is it not true that he characterises himself as an earnest member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is possible because he joined the SDS, I think, his wife and Mladen -- I do not know exactly the date -- simply out of some kind of fear, probably, because there were three parties at the time. The first in the territory of Prijedor or, rather, the former Bosnia-Herzegovina, first to be registered were SDA, HDZ. These were nationalist parties and afterwards the SDS was formed and it was logical that he would side with that party.
